newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom declines Eurobond report comment.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom declines Eurobond report comment.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly RAO Gazprom declined comment on Friday on a newspaper report that it planned to issue a Eurobond of up to $500 million.
The paper said Gazprom was set to become the first Russian company to tap the Eurobond market since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"Unfortunately, I cannot comment," the head of Gazprom's securities department Eduard Ivanov told Reuters, adding he could not discuss the matter until he had seen the article.
No other official at Gazprom, which last month raised $429.3 million with an issue of more than 30 million American Depositary Shares, was immediately available.
But bankers said it was early to talk of a Gazprom Eurobond.

"Talk of an imminent Gazprom bond is premature. Now they have done the equity deal, and due to their enormous financing requirements, people assume they will be a natural issuer for a Eurobond after Russia," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank.
"Gazprom is very unlikely to issue a deal this year. On the fastest schedule Russia's Eurobond will surface late November, which does not leave time for anyone else," he said.

Bankers said Gazprom had not yet asked banks to bid for a Eurobond mandate, but it already had close relationships with some banks such as Morgan Stanley, joint global coordinator for its ADS issue, and Dresdner Bank AG's Kleinwort Benson.
A Frankfurt-based investment banker said the maturity of a Gazprom issue could range from three to five years and the pricing would depend on the pricing of the Russia Eurobond issue.
"There are quite a few Russian corporates lining up, just look at the top corporates and they'll be looking."

Privatisation Minister Alfred Kokh said on Thursday that a 7.5 percent state-owned stake in national power company Unified Energy System would be sold off through an issue of convertible Eurobonds in the first half of December.
He gave no details of the issue but a 7.5 percent stake in UES would be worth some $260 million.
Analysts said the issue could spark the development of a Russian corporate bond market as firms sought to benefit from Russia's recently awarded credit rating.

Russian officials say the first sovereign Eurobond, expected to be worth up to $500 million, will be issued by the end of the year. Municipal authorities, including those of Moscow and St Petersburg, are also drawing up plans to tap Euromarkets.
